lesson.title: The Frequency a Circuit Chooses for Itself
lesson.summary: Natural frequency isolates the pace at which an LC pair would exchange energy forever if left undamped, a quantity set entirely by L and C, with resistance only pulling the observed ringing frequency slightly lower.
lesson.body:
The RLC circuit chapter introduced omega_0 = 1 over the square root of L times C as one of the two numbers controlling a circuit's ringing response, calling it the undamped natural frequency. This chapter isolates that quantity on its own: what it physically represents, why it depends only on L and C and not on R at all, and how damping shifts it into what is actually observed in a real circuit.

Physically, if a circuit's resistance were exactly zero, energy would slosh back and forth forever between the inductor's magnetic field and the capacitor's electric field with no losses. A fully charged capacitor drives current into the inductor, storing energy in its magnetic field. As the capacitor discharges through zero, the inductor's own current keeps flowing, by its very nature it resists changing, charging the capacitor back up with the opposite polarity, and the whole exchange reverses and repeats. The rate of that back and forth exchange, in radians per second, is exactly omega_0 = 1 over the square root of L times C, and the ordinary frequency in hertz is f_0 = omega_0 over (2 pi) = 1 over (2 pi times the square root of L times C). Resistance plays no part in setting that pace because resistance does not store energy at all, it only removes it over time, which is a separate question from how fast the ideal exchange would run.

Worked example: an LC pair has L = 1 millihenry, or 0.001 henries, and C = 100 nanofarads, or 0.0000001 farads. The product L times C is 0.001 times 0.0000001 = 0.0000000001, or 1e-10. Its square root is 1e-5. So omega_0 = 1 over 1e-5 = 100000 radians per second, and f_0 = 100000 over (2 pi) = 100000 divided by 6.2832, about 15915 hertz, roughly 15.9 kilohertz. Left undamped, this particular LC pair would naturally ring at just under 16 kilohertz.

Damping changes what is actually observed. Reusing the series RLC circuit's numbers from the previous chapter, R = 50 ohms, L = 0.1 henries, C = 10 microfarads, giving omega_0 = 1000 radians per second and zeta = 0.25, the circuit does not actually ring at exactly omega_0. The observed damped natural frequency is omega_d = omega_0 times the square root of (1 minus zeta squared) = 1000 times the square root of (1 minus 0.0625) = 1000 times the square root of 0.9375, about 1000 times 0.968, roughly 968 radians per second, or about 154 hertz, compared to the undamped 1000 radians per second, about 159 hertz. The heavier the damping, meaning the closer zeta gets to 1, the further the observed ringing frequency drops below omega_0, until at zeta = 1, critically damped, the ringing disappears entirely.

This is exactly the number engineers target when tuning a radio's resonant circuit, setting a crystal oscillator's reference frequency, or designing a filter's cutoff: choose L and C to place the natural frequency exactly where the circuit should want to operate, then use R, and therefore zeta, to control how sharply it responds there versus how much it rings once disturbed.
